title: Medigap Mistakes to Avoid: 2026 Enrollment Guide
excerpt: Learn the biggest Medigap mistakes to avoid, from missing enrollment windows to misunderstanding underwriting rules, so you can choose coverage with confidence.
author: David Haass
keyTakeaways: Medigap supplements Original Medicare, while Medicare Advantage replaces it entirely with a private plan
Your six-month Medigap Open Enrollment Period starts the month you turn 65 and have Part B, and missing it can trigger medical underwriting
Outside guaranteed issue windows, insurers can ask health questions and may charge more or deny coverage based on your medical history
Never cancel your current Medigap policy until your new policy is officially approved in writing
Medigap pricing follows community-rated, issue-age-rated, or attained-age-rated models, which affect how premiums change over time
seoTitle: Medigap Mistakes to Avoid: 2026 Enrollment Guide
seoDescription: Discover key Medigap mistakes to avoid, from enrollment timing to underwriting pitfalls, and enroll with confidence in 2026.

sections.text: Why Medigap Enrollment Feels So Overwhelming

sections.content: Plan A, Plan F, Plan G, Plan N. To someone new to Medicare, these letters read like a code nobody handed you the key to. Add in terms like guaranteed issue, underwriting, and open enrollment, and it is easy to feel stuck before you even start comparing options.
Timing matters more than most people realize, and a missed window can follow you for years. This guide breaks the Medigap decision into clear, manageable steps.
Once you know which mistakes to watch for, the process becomes far less intimidating.

sections.text: Medicare Terms That Trip People Up (And What They Actually Mean)

sections.content: One of the most common mix-ups is confusing Medigap with Medicare Advantage. They are not the same thing. Medigap supplements Original Medicare and helps pay leftover costs like coinsurance, while Medicare Advantage replaces Original Medicare with a private plan that often includes its own network and rules.

Plan letters simply describe standardized benefit packages. Plan G, for example, covers most gaps left by Original Medicare except the Part B deductible, while Plan N includes small copays for certain office and emergency room visits. One key difference between the two: Plan G covers Part B excess charges, the extra amount some providers can legally bill above the Medicare-approved amount, while Plan N does not, leaving you responsible for those excess charges if your provider charges them.

sections.calloutText: Guaranteed issue means an insurer must sell you a policy regardless of health history. Outside those protected windows, medical underwriting applies, meaning your health history can affect price or eligibility. According to Medicare.gov, guaranteed issue protections apply during specific windows defined by federal and state rules.

sections.content: A simple way to translate the jargon: ask what each term means for your specific doctors, prescriptions, and monthly budget. That personal lens turns confusing vocabulary into a decision you can actually make.

sections.text: Timing Mistakes That Cost You Money and Options

sections.content: Your [Medigap Open Enrollment Period](/faqs/medicare-supplement-open-enrollment/) lasts six months, starting the month you turn 65 and have Part B. During this window, insurers must sell you any Medigap policy they offer, without health questions. According to Medicare.gov, this six-month timeframe and the guaranteed issue protections that come with it are set by federal rule, so confirming your exact dates directly with Medicare.gov or CMS.gov is worthwhile.

sections.calloutText: If you miss this six-month period, insurers can require medical underwriting later. That means your health history could raise your premium or lead to a denial in most states. CMS.gov outlines the limited guaranteed issue situations that can still apply after your initial window closes, including trying a Medicare Advantage plan for the first time and deciding to switch back to Original Medicare within your trial right period, or moving out of your Medicare SELECT plan's service area.

sections.content: Turning 65 soon should trigger planning now, not a scramble later. If you delay enrollment because you still have employer coverage, confirm how that coverage coordinates with Medicare before your window closes.

Another frequent mistake is assuming you can [switch [Medigap plans](/faqs/what-is-a-medicare-supplement-plan-and-who-needs-one/)](/faqs/when-can-i-change-my-medicare-supplement-plan/) anytime without health questions. Outside guaranteed issue situations, switching almost always involves underwriting. That said, guaranteed issue rights are not limited to your initial enrollment window. Situations like exercising a Medicare Advantage trial right or moving out of a Medicare SELECT plan's service area can also let you switch Medigap plans without medical underwriting, so it is worth checking whether your specific situation qualifies before assuming underwriting is required.

sections.text: Underwriting Pitfalls: How Health Questions Can Get You Rejected or Overcharged

sections.content: Outside your guaranteed issue windows, insurers can ask detailed health questions before approving a Medigap application. This is standard practice in most states and is how carriers price risk.

Conditions like recent cancer treatment, heart disease, or certain chronic illnesses can lead to higher premiums or outright denial, depending on the insurer's underwriting guidelines. Rules vary by state and by company.
A costly mistake is canceling your current Medigap policy before receiving written approval on a new one. If the new application is denied, you could be left without supplemental coverage.

I always tell people to keep their current Medigap policy active until the new one is fully approved in writing. It costs a little extra to overlap coverage for a few weeks, but it protects you from a gap that could be far more expensive than a spare premium payment.

sections.text: Cost Confusion: Avoiding Surprise Premiums and Out-of-Pocket Expenses

sections.content: Medigap pricing generally follows one of three models: community-rated, issue-age-rated, or attained-age-rated. Community-rated plans charge everyone the same premium regardless of age, while attained-age-rated plans increase as you get older.

Choosing the lowest premium without checking a carrier's rate increase history is a common misstep. A plan that looks affordable today may rise sharply within a few years. It is also worth asking about additional ways to lower costs, such as a household discount some carriers offer when multiple people in the same home enroll in a Medigap policy, or considering high-deductible Plan G, which carries a much lower monthly premium in exchange for paying a higher annual deductible before the plan's benefits kick in.

sections.title: 2026 Part A and Part B Costs to Know
sections.footnote: Medigap can help cover many of these costs, but your Part B premium is separate and still your responsibility. Figures are published annually by CMS.gov; visit CMS.gov for the current official amounts.

sections.content: Medigap does not replace your Part B premium. It helps cover costs like coinsurance and deductibles that remain after Medicare pays its share. Compare total expected cost over several years, not just the sticker price of the monthly premium.

sections.text: Making Sure Your Doctors and Prescriptions Stay Covered

sections.content: Medigap works differently from Medicare Advantage when it comes to doctor access. With most [Medigap plans](/faqs/what-is-a-medicare-supplement-plan-and-who-needs-one/), you can see any provider who accepts Medicare nationwide, without needing referrals or network approval.
Medigap does not include prescription drug coverage. If you need help paying for medications, you will likely want a standalone Part D plan alongside your Medigap policy.

sections.calloutText: Confirm three things: your doctors accept Medicare, your prescriptions are covered under a separate Part D plan, and your chosen Medigap letter fits your expected care needs.

sections.content: Not all [Medigap plans](/faqs/what-is-a-medicare-supplement-plan-and-who-needs-one/) work identically, even though benefits are standardized by letter. Assuming every plan behaves the same with any provider is a mistake worth avoiding before you sign anything. It is also worth remembering that Plan G and Plan N handle Part B excess charges differently, so if you tend to see providers who do not accept Medicare assignment, that difference can affect your out-of-pocket costs.

sections.text: A Step-by-Step Comparison Process to Enroll With Confidence

items: Assess your health needs, budget, and how often you expect to see doctors or specialists
Compare plan letters based on what they cover, not just their name recognition
Check the pricing structure and rate increase history for each carrier you are considering
Confirm your enrollment timing to protect guaranteed issue rights
Review your prescription needs against available Part D plans

sections.content: Working with a licensed Medicare agent can add clarity at each step, without adding pressure to decide on the spot. A transparent conversation should explain your options clearly and answer your questions directly.

Real client reviews and clear explanations about how help works are good signs you are speaking with a trustworthy source. A comparison process focused on your needs, not a sales quota, is what leads to lasting confidence in your choice.

sections.text: Frequently Asked Questions About Avoiding Medigap Mistakes

faqs.question: I feel like I need more time before I talk to anyone about Medigap. Is that okay?
faqs.answer: Taking time to learn is reasonable and encouraged. Just make sure you understand key deadlines, like your six-month Medigap Open Enrollment Period, so you protect your options while you review information at your own pace.

faqs.question: Will I get a pushy sales call if I ask questions about Medigap plans?
faqs.answer: Licensed agents are expected to explain options clearly without pressuring you to decide immediately. A transparent, no-obligation conversation should focus on answering your questions, and you control the pace of any discussion.

faqs.question: Can I just research Medigap on my own before deciding?
faqs.answer: Self-research is a good first step and can help you understand the basics. Underwriting rules and state-specific nuances are often where independent research falls short, so pairing your research with a licensed expert's review helps confirm accuracy.

faqs.question: How do I know which online sources about Medigap I can trust?
faqs.answer: Look for plain language, clear licensing information, and transparent explanations of how help works. Real client reviews add confidence, and cross-checking details against official resources like medicare.gov's Medigap overview or CMS.gov helps verify accuracy, especially for specific rules like the six-month enrollment window and guaranteed issue protections.

sections.content: The biggest Medigap mistakes tend to fall into four categories: mistimed enrollment, underwriting surprises, cost confusion, and coverage gaps with doctors or prescriptions. Each one is avoidable once you know where to look.
A step-by-step comparison approach, built around your needs and timeline, leads to a choice you can feel confident about long after you enroll.
Seek out clear, transparent guidance rather than deciding under pressure. A calm, informed decision today can protect your coverage and budget for years to come.
